entry.title: Why Emmy Wins and Hollywood Recognition Don’t Guarantee Jobs for BIPOC Artists: ‘The Needle Has Not F***ing Moved’
entry.summary: IndieWire talks to BIPOC talent below- and above-the-line to address the opportunity gaps in Hollywood.
entry.content:
Get the agent, book the studio job, win the award, and so on, collecting infinity stones like Thanos until you can buy that dream house in that quaint part of Studio City. For many working filmmakers, especially women and people of color, the realities of making it in Hollywood are even more nuanced. Recognition can get you into the room, but it does not necessarily get your movie made.

Bridget Stokes knows this distinction intimately. When she became the first Black woman to win an Emmy for directing a variety series in 2022 (“A Black Lady Sketch Show”), meetings followed, and congratulations poured in from every angle. She says the award may have earned her more sit-downs when she reached out, but it didn’t produce the career acceleration outsiders might expect. “I didn’t get a [studio] job offer for almost four years after I had won the award,” Stokes said. “Like four years after I had won an Emmy and had this decoration, I never got a job offer.”

Related Stories
From ‘The Devils’ to ‘Obsession,’ How ‘Femcel’ Horror Handles Horny Women
Walter Koenig, Actor Who Played Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90

Her experience comes amid a contraction that has made an already difficult business considerably harder. According to a Film LA 2025 Q4 and year-to-date Film Production Report, Los Angeles on-location production fell 16.1 percent in 2025. Every major category declined, including student films, shorts, documentaries, and music videos. At the end of 2025, television production was 50.1 percent below its five-year average and feature films were 31.7 percent below.

The coronavirus pandemic, major labor strikes in the entertainment and media industry, mega mergers like Skydance, and the 2025 wildfires have played a major role in these declines. Though Film LA’s 2026 Q1 report shows an uptick from recent lows, production remains far below historical levels.

“There’s No Place You Can Reach and Have Made It”

Stokes’ experience also complicates one of Hollywood’s most enduring ideas about success — that it’s linear, and that careers operate like ladders. Climb high enough and eventually you reach a level where getting the next project greenlit becomes easier. “There’s no place you can reach and have made it,” Stokes said. She has spoken with Oscar-nominated directors and established auteurs who still struggle to finance passion projects. “We’re artists trying to convince commerce people to make our art. It’s just never going to be easy, no matter who you are.” Stokes wrote and will direct her upcoming project “Zugzwang,” a film noir political thriller starring Christina Elmore as Lady, a Black female private detective and former child soldier.

Who originates the work can tell you who will get the jobs. In her 2026 report, Boxed In, author Martha M. Lauzen of the Center for the Study of Women in Television and Film at San Diego University, found that programs with at least one woman creator employed substantially more women in other key creative positions. Women wrote 48 percent of episodes on those programs, compared with just 17 percent on programs created exclusively by men. The report says women accounted for just 22 percent of creators across broadcast and streaming television in the 2025-26 season.

These pressures are creating a new slate of indie filmmakers who aren’t posting eulogies to Hollywood on Threads or waiting for the good old days to return. They are finding investors, building production companies, making smaller projects, cultivating core audiences and collaborating with one another. In some cases, they are questioning whether the traditional markers of Hollywood success should remain the destination at all.

Producer Ebony Elaine Hardin has spent enough time inside both systems to see the contrast. Hardin began in casting, working for companies including CBS and NBCUniversal and casting directors Francine Maisler and Carmen Cuba before moving into production. Today, she is director of production at Dropout, an independent, subscriber-funded comedy network, studio, and distributor.

“We kind of dropped out of the studio system,” Hardin said tongue-in-cheek. Instead of trying to meet the expectations of a larger corporate owner, the company chose something smaller, more creatively autonomous, and able to craft programs for its audience.

That model challenges another assumption of the traditional system. Must everything appeal to everybody in order to be successful? “I don’t think that entertainment personally has to do that,” Hardin said. “It can be more niche.” She said the independent model can start with a smaller community. “This is just for these people,” made by people who care deeply about that audience. If the work eventually crosses over, all the better.

In 2025, just one in 10 of Hollywood’s top theatrical films had a woman director, while roughly one in five had a director of color, according to UCLA’s 2026 Hollywood Diversity Report for theatrical feature films. The numbers get worse when you count all credited writers. BIPOC writers accounted for just 13.5 percent of the 185 writers for top theatrical releases, while women accounted for 19.5 percent. 71.9 percent of all credited writers were white men.

Vietnam-born actor Trieu Tran, who immigrated to Canada and was raised in Boston, has been working professionally for 25 years. He said this year marked his first time working with a Vietnamese filmmaker. He has worked on cult classics like “How High” and “Tropic Thunder,” spent two-and-a-half seasons on HBO’s “The Newsroom,” built a substantial theater career in such works as “Equus,” where he played Alan Strang alongside East West Players co-star George Takei, earning a Los Angeles Drama Critics Circle (LADCC) nomination, and even once flew to Thailand for the independent feature “Trade of Innocence” opposite Oscar-winning actress Mira Sorvino in 2011.

The film gave him a prominent supporting role as Duke, the antagonist. “I’m in Thailand with Dermot Mulroney and Mira Sorvino. The three of us, making this film for two months. I’m thinking, hey, you know, now here’s my chance,” Tran recalled. He returned home hoping the film would succeed, but it didn’t find its audience. “You come back, and the film was not a success for myriads of reasons,” Tran said.

He had no clear next steps to take. “I’m booking the jobs. All my coworkers are telling me I’m a good actor. I do theater. All the critics are loving my work. Audiences are loving my work, and I’m just like, I don’t know what I need to do to get to that next sort of level, and then ‘The Newsroom’ happened.” After the 2012 Aaron Sorkin series, Tran worked on S1 of “Altered Carbon” as series regular “Mr. Leung” in 2018, and then starred as “Sharko” in Hulu’s 2020 anthology “Monsterland.”

In a SYFY WIRE interview, show creator, executive producer and writer Mary Laws said of Tran, “I think that he’s a phenomenal actor who just has not gotten his day and I think that that’s part of the inherent racism in Hollywood. And we, as a writers’ room, fought really hard to make sure that we cast a Vietnamese actor in that role as a Vietnamese trawler.” Since the show, Tran hasn’t had any acting work — in film or TV — outside of theater.

The Needle Only Moves for a Select Few

To be clear, making a living as an artist is precarious for actors of any race. But actors of color, Tran said, start with a bigger mountain to climb, with fewer roles available and many still constrained by stereotypes. Casting feedback can become almost absurdly specific: “Too Asian, not Asian enough. Too Vietnamese, not Vietnamese enough,” he said. “I hate when I hear people say the needle is moving. The needle has not fucking moved. We need to stop saying that. It’s only moving for a select few.”

BIPOC performers made up only 23.1 percent of leads in top theatrical films in 2025 despite comprising 45.2 percent of the U.S. population, according to UCLA’s report. Asian actors made up just 3.7 percent of that lead slice. When young actors ask Tran for advice, he tells them, “There is literally no blueprint. There’s luck involved…not quitting, getting the opportunity, and finally getting the sheer luck. There’s so many intangibles why you get cast and don’t cast. And a lot of time, it really has nothing to do with talent.”

Emmy-winning casting director Jazzy Collins has watched the traditional markers of achievement lose some of their predictive power. She is the first Black woman to win the Emmy for Outstanding Reality Casting. She said an award gives her name “a little bit more weight,” particularly among people accustomed to the traditional Hollywood hierarchy. But she has also watched digital creators build lucrative careers without ever appearing on a network television show.

“There’s some really fantastic people that have never won an Oscar, never won an Emmy, and they’re working more than the people that have,” Collins said. She isn’t dismissive of those honors. “I am so thankful for it,” she said of her own recognition. Rather, she believes the traditional markers of what makes you good in this industry are changing.

“This Hustle Doesn’t Stop Just Because You Meet Five Investors”

So Collins has spent years learning another, rarely romanticized part of filmmaking: fundraising. She has deliberately sought out investors, learned how to discuss financial structures, and built relationships with people interested in financing films. Work that, she said, never really ends. “This hustle doesn’t stop just because you meet five investors,” Collins said. In doing that work, she arrived at her current philosophy, “I’m not gonna wait for you to knock on my door. You’re gonna have to come knock on my door when I’m already up and running.”

Filmmaker Lauri Levenfeld shares the same sentiment. “I’ve always been extremely scrappy and known that I’ve got to participate in many ways to make a project happen,” said the writer-director who got her start in film as a cinematographer. Levenfeld will direct her feature “Swipe Up,” a southern-gothic horror dark comedy about a deadly sorority competition, while also producing Stokes’ “Zugzwang.” For emerging filmmakers, Levenfeld argues, a good script and financing aren’t enough. “You have to literally think about from A to Z how you’re going to get this thing done.”

Former Netflix executive and producer Wayne Horton offers an important counterweight to the romance of going independent. “Studios have become increasingly risk-averse,” he said, “because executives are under enormous pressure to make projects that work.” Familiar stars and proven filmmakers offer some protection against that risk, but the result can be fewer opportunities for people without many credits. Independent filmmakers cannot ignore those economics either.

“There are a lot of great scripts out there, but there isn’t a strong business case for every script,” Horton said. “My job as a producer is to develop projects that are great creatively, but also turn a profit.” With so many entertainment options, viewers have become extremely segmented. To have a sustainable career in this business, Horton said, he has to develop work that speaks directly to specific audiences. Horton is developing several projects, including a high school rom-com starring Marsai Martin and an ensemble comedy with Emmy winner Lamorne Morris attached.

Is the Answer in Indies?

The data suggests these audiences are a big part of the business. BIPOC moviegoers bought the majority of opening-weekend tickets for five of the top 10 and 11 of the top 20 films at the global box office in 2025, plus half the tickets for another film, according to the UCLA report, and the theatrical films with casts that were 41–50 percent BIPOC produced the highest median global and domestic box office.

And filmmakers building outside Hollywood’s traditional gates aren’t rejecting the business. Increasingly, they are learning more of it themselves. Who is the audience? How much should the film cost? Where does the financing come from? How will people find it? And the question most recently making headlines: Who owns what they create?

Hardin once viewed success through traditional Hollywood milestones, but now has a broader sense of what a creative career looks like. These days she’s more focused on making work she cares about with a community she wants to work alongside.

“I know incredibly talented writers and directors with phenomenal stories,” she said. And as creative producer and executive at her company 903 Entertainment, she’s championing “Flacalta Effect,” a satirical zombie movie in which an Ozempic-like drug triggers a zombie apocalypse, written and directed by Rochae Jeffrey and featuring an all-POC cast, and “Trashy People,” a coming-of-age story about a young woman working at her college recycling center to pay for school, written and directed by Marissa High.

Hardin hasn’t given up on the accolades either. She still wants the Emmy. She still submits projects to Sundance and SXSW. She still intends to knock on those doors, but no longer believes she has to wait behind them. “I’m just going to keep knocking until I get my moment,” Hardin said. A moment she’s certain will come through independent work.

And the data supports her confidence. According to feature film data from Film LA’s Q1 2026 production report, feature production rose 52.3 percent year over year in Q1 2026, from 451 to 687 shoot days, and was actually 20.6 percent above the five-year average. Most of that quarter’s feature-film activity came from independent films.

The revolution will likely be built on an indie budget (including equitable backend for all involved), and it just might get a theatrical release before it goes to streaming. The heavily guarded industry gates will likely never fling open, but with filmmakers now understanding exactly how high the mountain is, they are much better poised to build another path up.

Chaseedaw Giles is a Los Angeles-based journalist, screenwriter, and filmmaker.

entry.title: From ‘The Devils’ to ‘Obsession,’ How ‘Femcel’ Horror Handles Horny Women
entry.summary: Horror has always been fearfully fascinated with female desire. Now, offscreen, women are questioning whether real romance is worth wanting at all.
entry.content:
Has sexual violence always been a spectator sport? It certainly has an audience. Last week, prediction market Polymarket removed a contract that allowed users to bet on whether any of the seven men accused of sexually assaulting a Cornell University student in an alleged gang rape would face felony sex-crime charges.

The men have broadly denied the allegations, and no one has been criminally charged. But before the Polymarket contract came down, bets about the Cornell case generated more than $450,000 in trading volume — suggesting that just the prospect of accountability for claims of alleged sexual violence can be repackaged and sold as dark entertainment today.

Related Stories
Walter Koenig, Actor Who Played Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
How ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Used Vintage ‘Godfather’ Lenses to Capture NYC on Location

Ken Russell’s “The Devils” understood the power of that spectacle 55 years ago. Now enjoying an extended theatrical run following its long-awaited restoration, the notorious 1971 film reveals how readily powerful institutions can turn women’s private experiences into public theater. In Russell’s feverish account of religious repression, a nun’s unrequited lust for a priest becomes a political weapon: a message that’s only grown more resonant in an era of increasing cruelty online.

In the decades since, horror hasn’t stopped asking what happens when women want too much. If anything, the cultural fascination with female rage has made those questions more urgent and their resolutions more complicated. From Curry Barker’s “Obsession” to Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” this year has produced a striking collection of women whose desires — and other people’s attempts to control them — become sources of terror, humiliation, and transformation.

The internet’s evolving concept of the “femcel” label offers a provocative lens through which to reconsider these characters, even if none fits its original definition of a woman denied romantic or sexual satisfaction particularly well. Offscreen, meanwhile, women are asking another question: What if the intimate relationships they’ve been taught to want aren’t worth wanting at all?

Our Lady of Unrequited Lust

Played with delirious conviction by Vanessa Redgrave, Sister Jeanne is a hunchbacked nun whose devotion to God takes a backseat to her passion for Father Grandier (Oliver Reed).

Confined to a convent and ashamed of her body, Jeanne escapes into elaborate sexual fantasies about the handsome priest, imagining herself without her spinal deformity in a very public and passionate embrace. But Sister Jeanne doesn’t just want Grandier. She wants him to want her, and her conviction that he never will drives her toward increasingly destructive delusions.

In the renewed online conversation surrounding “The Devils,” most of the overt thirst has understandably been reserved for Reed’s rakish priest. “I would let Father Grandier do unspeakable things to me,” declared one of many, many Reddit users speaking to that theme.

Redgrave’s simultaneously sympathetic and villainous Sister Jeanne has inspired a more complicated fascination. “Sister Jeanne was the first femcel,” proclaimed one Letterboxd user after an October 17 screening.

Fifty-five years after her cinematic debut, Jeanne has become something like the patron saint of femcels. She’s lonely, sexually frustrated, and painfully conscious of her perceived undesirability. She’s also manipulative, vindictive, and complicit in a man’s destruction. Redgrave refuses to make either side easy to dismiss. Jeanne’s longing is pitiable, but its consequences are appalling.

Russell, however, is interested in more than watching a woman go mad with desire. Jeanne’s accusations of demonic possession become politically useful to authorities determined to destroy Grandier, transforming her private anguish into an elaborate public performance. Even as she helps persecute the object of her obsession, Jeanne is herself raped under the guise of an exorcism, subjected to invasive sexualized rituals by the very men exploiting her testimony. Her culpability doesn’t erase her victimhood, nor does her victimhood absolve her.

From the repressed Sister Ruth in “Black Narcissus” to the ostracized Carrie White and the desperately lonely heroine of “May,” horror has long made monsters of women whose desires exceed their circumstances. Their afflictions have been called everything from hysteria to demonic possession. Today, some viewers recognize them as cinematic femcels. (Hell, even Zendaya’s Emma in Kristoffer Borgli’s “The Drama” — a bullied teenager who once planned a school shooting — invites a more ideological reading of the archetype, her isolation having curdled into fantasies of violent revenge.)

Ironically, the term “incel” itself originated with a woman. In 1997, a queer Canadian known as Alana founded an inclusive online community for people struggling to find sex and romance. Over time, male-dominated forums appropriated the label, and Elliot Rodger’s 2014 killing spree in Isla Vista helped make it synonymous with violent misogyny. Some male incels even rejected the legitimacy of female romantic frustration, arguing that women could always obtain sex by lowering their standards.

Women helped create the language of romantic exclusion, only to find themselves excluded from it. Never mind that finding someone willing to sleep with you is hardly the same as finding someone who loves, respects, or even attracts you.

Nor are femcels simply female versions of violent male incels. A 2024 study by Hannah Rae Evans and Adam Lankford found that femcel discussions showed less support for aggression and violence than researchers had documented among male incels.

Then TikTok got involved. As researchers Jacob Johanssen and Jilly Boyce Kay explain, “femcelcore” transformed romantic exclusion into an often-ironic aesthetic of loneliness, resentment, self-loathing, and feminine rage. Literal femceldom and its more fashionable online performance are related but distinct phenomena, though popular culture increasingly treats them as interchangeable.

What began as an identity for women who felt fundamentally undesirable became an aesthetic that made their alienation seem desirable. Whether anyone is getting better at understanding them is another question.

The Monsters Men Make

Curry Barker’s “Obsession” takes the nightmare of unrequited love and turns it inside out.

Bear (Michael Johnston) is a romantically hopeless young man who uses a magical trinket to make his crush, Nikki (Inde Navarrette), fall hopelessly in love with him. It works a little too well. Nikki becomes the ultimate nightmare girlfriend: clingy, jealous, sexually insatiable, and eventually murderous. Her transformation recalls a long cinematic tradition of obsessive women, from “Fatal Attraction” to “Misery.”

But Barker’s clever reversal is that Nikki’s desires aren’t actually hers, and the monster is entirely of Bear’s making. Where Sister Jeanne’s authentic longing becomes a weapon for powerful men, Bear eliminates Nikki’s autonomy altogether. He wants the rewards of romance without the inconvenience of another person’s free will. Even after discovering the horrifying consequences of his wish, Bear struggles to relinquish control.

The real horror in “Obsession” isn’t a woman who loves too much, but a man who believes being loved is something he’s owed. Barker makes the violation literal when Bear has sex with Nikki after discovering that his wish has effectively imprisoned her inside her own body. The scene is rape, even if the enchanted version of Nikki appears willing. And her vacant, tearful expression makes clear that the real woman has no say in what’s happening to her.

Across five decades, “The Devils” and “Obsession” arrive at the same particularly ugly irony: Women portrayed as dangerous for wanting too much ultimately become victims of men who believe their bodies are available for the taking.

Actual femcels, meanwhile, appear considerably less frightening than their fictional counterparts. A 2026 study by Brandon Sparks and Alexandra Zidenberg compared 61 self-identified femcels with 58 other women, finding elevated levels of sexual depression, anxiety, and dissatisfaction among the former. Particularly striking was their fear of abuse by potential partners. The small, demographically uneven samples limit broader conclusions, but the irony is difficult to ignore: While horror imagines sexually frustrated women as people to fear, some of the real women behind the label are themselves afraid of being hurt.

Plus, loneliness doesn’t necessarily mean desperation. According to Pew Research Center, only 35 percent of single American women were actively looking for a relationship or casual dates in 2022, compared with half of single men. Enjoying single life and having other priorities were among the leading explanations offered by single Americans who weren’t looking. Not every woman without a partner considers herself deprived of one.

That distinction became politically charged after Donald Trump’s reelection in 2024, when some American women expressed interest in South Korea’s 4B movement, which rejects dating men, heterosexual marriage, sex with men, and childbirth. Born from feminist resistance to misogyny and sexual violence, 4B treats abstention not as romantic failure but as an exercise of autonomy. Its American visibility hardly established a mass exodus from heterosexuality, but it revealed something about the appeal of opting out.

Here, the language of femceldom begins to break down. Women who want relationships but cannot find them aren’t the same as women who no longer consider those relationships worth pursuing. Amid growing discussions of “heteropessimism,” or disillusionment with the promises of heterosexuality, the difference between being unwanted and refusing to participate matters more than ever.

And for a genre that has spent decades imagining women’s unsatisfied desires as a threat, that opens up some interesting possibilities.

What If She Never Wants Him?

For Kris Williams (Hannah Einbinder), the object of her obsession is already a horror movie.

In Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma,” the young queer director is hired to revive a slasher franchise she’s worshipped since childhood. Her first priority is finding Billy Presley (Gillian Anderson), the reclusive actress who played its original final girl. Kris has spent years experiencing desire at a safe remove, through other people’s images. Meeting Billy threatens to collapse the distance between watching and wanting.

Like Sister Jeanne, she’s fixated on someone seemingly beyond her reach. Unlike Jeanne, she might actually get to find out what happens next.

The franchise has its own messy history. Once protested by the religious right, “Camp Miasma” is now considered transphobic, thanks to its gender-nonconforming killer. Enter Kris, hired to give the aging property a suitably progressive makeover. Yesterday’s moral panic is today’s branding opportunity.

Schoenbrun’s satire cuts in both directions. The studio cares little about the franchise’s ugliness or its pleasures, beyond whatever might make a reboot profitable. Kris, inconveniently, understands that making something politically acceptable isn’t necessarily the same as understanding its appeal.

This tension extends beyond Schoenbrun’s fictional studio. Barker’s “Obsession” has earned more than $520 million worldwide, compared with roughly $8.7 million for “Camp Miasma.” Their vastly different theatrical releases make those grosses an imperfect referendum on audience tastes, but the disparity illustrates how differently the industry markets stories about desire. Female obsession is profitable. Female autonomy is a harder pitch.

Billy knows more about that distinction than her admirer realizes. She reveals that an encounter previously understood as sex was, for her, an experience of sexual violence. The fantasy Kris treasured as a fan means something very different to the woman who lived it. Suddenly, the gap between the image and the person inside it becomes impossible to ignore.

Schoenbrun doesn’t suggest that desire can erase trauma. Instead, Kris and Billy’s growing intimacy makes room for something transformative: the freedom to explore fantasies without surrendering the right to decide what happens to their bodies. For once, the question isn’t whether a woman wants too much, but whether she gets to decide what she wants in the first place.

There’s a visual kinship with Russell, too. Derek Jarman’s blinding white architecture makes “The Devils” a cathedral of repression, while Schoenbrun’s candy-colored gore and hand-painted backdrops turn “Camp Miasma” into an ecstatic playground. Both directors abandon realism to give desire a world of its own.

But where Russell’s world turns longing into persecution, Schoenbrun lets it become a creative force. When Kris’s increasingly personal ideas clash with the studio’s plans, it looks less like a defeat than a beginning. Reclaiming horror, it turns out, might require more than giving an old franchise a new coat of paint.

Female rage became a lucrative entertainment category by making women’s anger legible as power. Femcelcore sells something slipperier: the misery of being unwanted as an identity other people might actually desire. Neither transformation settles the question of who profits from women’s pain, much less who gets to control its meaning.

For Sister Jeanne, wanting a man she cannot have becomes the engine of her destruction. For Nikki, being wanted by a man who refuses to accept her autonomy is just as catastrophic. Kris and Billy offer a more liberating possibility: desire needn’t end in possession, punishment, or even the conventional romance women have spent centuries being told to pursue.

The point isn’t that horror needs to become gentler, or that its ugliest fantasies should disappear. It’s that women deserve the freedom to make, watch, and reclaim these movies on their own terms.

It’s easy to picture Kris and Billy taking in a screening of “The Devils” on date night. But would they recognize themselves in Sister Jeanne? Pity her? Laugh at her? Maybe they’d just admire Russell’s outrageous imagery. Either way, the thought of two women, on a date, watching a nun want too much — and enjoying themselves immensely — feels like heaven.

From Warner Bros. Clockwork, “Ken Russell’s The Devils” is in theaters now.

entry.title: Walter Koenig, Actor Who Played Chekov on ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
entry.summary: Walter Koenig, who played Anton Chekov on ‘Star Trek,' dies at 90.
entry.content:
Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Andreievich Chekov, a key member of the U.S.S. Enterprise on the original “Star Trek” series and across the first seven films, has died. He was 90.

As Chekov, a Russian crew member, Koenig spoke in a thick, almost exaggerrated accent and sported a Davy Jones “moptop”. His presence on the bridge was a reminder of Gene Roddenberry’s utopian vision. The original “Star Trek” aired during the height of the Cold War, but it imagined a future in which such regional conflicts had ended in the name of space exploration. Koenig first joined the starship in the show’s second season and would go on to appear in 36 episodes. He would later voice now-President Chekov in 2023’s “Star Trek: Picard.”

Related Stories
How ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Used Vintage ‘Godfather’ Lenses to Capture NYC on Location
‘Queen at Sea’ Review: Juliette Binoche Guides Director Lance Hammer Back to Screens with a Searing Film About Dementia and Consent

On the big screen, Chekov was usually a bit player, though he did play a key role in “Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan.” His character’s scouting trip ends with Khan (Ricardo Montalbán) freed from exile and back in control of a space vessel.

Koenig’s film credits include “Goodbye, Raggedy Ann” and “Babylon 5.” In addition to acting, Koenig was a screenwriter who worked on such shows as “Land of the Lost,” “Family,” and “What Really Happened to the Class of ’65?.” He wrote several memoirs and was appeared frequently at Star Trek conventions.

“I was always very pleased when we were shooting the show and the motion pictures, to be identified with ‘Star Trek,'” Koenig said in a 2020 interview with Trekmovie.com. “I thought we were putting forward some very trenchant socio-political philosophies that needed to be articulated. I think we did that by projecting problems that were current into the future where it was more admissible. I was always pleased that we were dealing with issues of mankind and humanity and how we can achieve a better moral society and be inclusive of all races, creeds, sexes, philosophies, etcetera.”

entry.title: How ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Used Vintage ‘Godfather’ Lenses to Capture NYC on Location
entry.summary: DP Sam Levy tells IndieWire about designing a throwback look for "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York" with the help of some vintage lenses.
entry.content:
John Turturro and cinematographer Sam Levy hadn’t worked together before, both signing onto Noah Segan’s “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” but they did have something in common. Levy came up as a camera assistant under the great Harris Savides, who also shot Turturro in “Margot at the Wedding.” They’d both gotten close to Savides and had all kinds of stories that gave the actor and DP a nice shared language to work on this throwback crime thriller about a thief named Harry (Turturro) who steals from the wrong vape goon (Will Price) and has one last, desperate chance to make good.

But Levy also had something tangible.

Related Stories
‘Queen at Sea’ Review: Juliette Binoche Guides Director Lance Hammer Back to Screens with a Searing Film About Dementia and Consent
‘Clayface’ Tops the Box Office with $24 Million. What Does It Signal About DC Studios’ Latest Reboot?

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” was shot primarily with a set of Bausch & Lomb Super Baltar lenses — the same set, in fact, that cinematographer Gordon Willis used to shoot “The Godfather.” But Savides also owned an even older set of original Baltar lenses that Levy brought to bless the set. “I carried Harris’ lenses with us,” Levy told IndieWire. “They’re very similar but had just a little bit of a different flavor, and they had a different focal length. Some of them had kind of in-between focal lengths. So, it was convenient, but it also just felt nice to have a piece of Harris.”

It’s especially nice for the eyes of the project, the lenses, to have history and lineage on a movie like “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York.” Segan’s thriller takes as its central dramatic question the tension between the analog and the digital, the New York that’s coming into being in the 2020s and the New York that’s disintegrating to bring it to life. And Levy really wanted to lean into that, visually.

“[The Super Baltars] have these aberrations in them which put off a lot of people. They vignette and they flare in a way that is very beautiful but you can’t — it’s hard [to control. For example, if you shoot with the iris wide open, they completely fall apart, and they look soft, but not in a pleasing way. Harris Savides used them on ‘Margot at the Wedding,’ which John is in. And at that time, I remember having a lot of conversations with [Savides] about how difficult they were,” Levy said.

But after doing some camera tests with Turturro and seeing how he looked through those lenses, Levy found a sweet spot that’s weathered and alluring, with a clarity that is purposeful but never too sharp or soulless. The flaws and the aberrations the lenses created were, in fact, Levy’s favorite parts. “It’s an urgent necessity to take risks when you’re a cinematographer and to try things that are maybe on the edge of being too dark or underexposed. I played a lot with that in this film, with silhouette,” Levy said.

This is especially true in the Bronx apartment that Harry shares with his wife Rosie (Karina Arroyave), trapped in a hospital bed in what New Yorker realtors would call a “prewar” building and what most New Yorkers would call “don’t trust that elevator to work.” Levy spent a lot of time there, trying to see and absorb the character of the space, not to correct it with lighting, but to see how it could help tell the story through how his camera captured it.

“ You open the door, you see the hallway; you close the door, it’s completely dark, and I knew so much happens in that little stretch. And I had to really spend time there to get to a place where it’s like, ‘Oh, when he comes home, he’ll emerge out of the darkness,” Levy said.

Levy also worked with production designer Rocío Giménez to arrange the space so we felt the transition and the invasion of Harry’s home when it happens. How can that conflict pop in the frame before the actors even start speaking?

“I suggested, ‘Why don’t we put a picture up and we see the guys in the reflection?’” Levy said. “It’s got to be at a very particular angle, and then we’ve got to light them so that you can really see [the goons in the next room], but we’re panning from John. It really was all in one. So that was really fun, but it was very painstaking to plot that out, and I worked very closely with Rocío Giménez, our great production designer, and our art director, Rosa Callejas, on being able to get that,” Levy said.

Giménez told IndieWire that her goal was to make sure Harry and Rosie’s apartment reflected a home that had history, and therefore room for all those hidden surprise angles, too. “It needed to feel textured — in the objects, in the layers of paint — and never remodeled. Things break, walls chip, and those marks accumulate over time. We also wanted the apartment to feel very warm, almost glowing. Although the apartment was a location, we transformed it extensively: reworking parts of the kitchen, adding wallpaper, repainting, and building walls to make the space feel smaller,” Giménez said.

Giménez and her team also made adjustments to make the home invasion look properly invasive, scattering even more objects around every time we cut back to it. But it took a real team effort to craft that sense of lived history that imbues every frame of “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” and especially those sequences in Harry’s apartment. Giménez, Levy, and Segan all talked about it extensively, and then, at a certain point, let their New York location have its say, too.

“When you’re working on a location — sometimes you don’t have the time, but it takes time to acclimate to the environment. And one thing I really learned from Harris Savides, that he would always say to me when, a few times, I got to operate for him, ‘Just look. Take a look at what you’re doing. Look at it. Don’t frame it up. Just sit there and look,’” Levy said.

It’s apt, then, that Savides’ lenses were on Turturro, right alongside Levy’s.

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” is now playing in theaters.

entry.title: ‘Queen at Sea’ Review: Juliette Binoche Guides Director Lance Hammer Back to Screens with a Searing Film About Dementia and Consent
entry.summary: Lance Hammer's first film in nearly two decades, 'Queen at Sea,' stars Juliette Binoche as the daughter of a dementia-addled woman. Review.
entry.content:
Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. Greenwich Entertainment releases “Queen at Sea” in theaters starting Friday, October 30.

Lance Hammer was the toast of the town in 2008 with his hard-hitting, Mississippi-set coming-of-age drama “Ballast.” The Dardennes-esque vérité portrait of lives careening from loss and economic hardship won two awards at the Sundance Film Festival that year — including Best Director for Hammer — and received multiple Film Independent Spirit and Gotham award nominations.

And then, poof: Hammer was never heard from again.

He has now returned, almost two decades later, with an extremely upsetting but compassionate moral drama about agency amid dementia, titled “Queen at Sea.” It stars Juliette Binoche as a woman desperate and panicked to take care of her ailing mother, Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall, absolutely shattering in her specificity toward the sickness’ toll), who is slipping deeper into the illness. Leslie’s grasp of time, memory, and function is vanishing in the multi-story London flat she shares with her husband of 19 years, Martin (a brutally heartbreaking Tom Courtenay). Meanwhile, Amanda (Binoche), an academic on sabbatical, is going through a separation herself — from her husband in Newcastle, and now she’s forced to bring her daughter, Sara (Florence Hunt), with her back to London to check in on her mother.

Related Stories
‘Clayface’ Tops the Box Office with $24 Million. What Does It Signal About DC Studios’ Latest Reboot?
Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores Huge $19.5 Million Second Weekend

But when Amanda catches her stepfather, Martin, in a compromising position with Leslie, another separation sets into motion, with Leslie potentially about to be lost in an elder-care system that’s frightening and scary for the patient, and a kind of emotional death sentence for her and her loved ones.

As someone who’s watched a close loved one lose themselves to Alzheimer’s disease, I found “Queen at Sea” to be especially bruising, even despite some of its patchier plot notes. The emotions are there, even if the story is, well, lost at sea at times. The geographical configuration surrounding Amanda, having left behind a husband (and Sara’s father) in Newcastle, is confusing. Meanwhile, Sara has very quickly restarted her life in Newcastle with new friends and a potential new flame, as writer/director Hammer draws parallel comparisons in the edit between Sara’s blooming relationship with a classmate, and Leslie’s mental deterioration and estrangement from her own partner.

When the movie begins, Amanda is on a house call to check on Leslie, and walks in on Martin attempting to have sex with a dazed-out, addled-eyed Leslie prostrate on the bed. This is not the first time this has happened, and it’s an occurrence Amanda has implored Martin to knock off. But the Viagra in his medicine cabinet suggests otherwise, that he keeps going back for more, that Amanda keeps asking him to stop.

Dementia dramas like Sarah Polley’s wounding “Away from Her” (wherein Julie Christie’s husband Grant Anderson basically sets her up in a nursing home to counteract his own infidelities) and Michael Haneke’s Oscar-winning “Amour” (the harshest of this fleet of films) tend to center close-up on the relations between an Alzheimer’s patient and her partner, and how these relationships break down when there are fewer past and present memories to found them on.

Hammer’s film introduces profound new questions and issues about consent into the formula — is Leslie agreeing on some level to have sex with her husband? Is the only pleasure in her winnowing life to be denied? Can a person with dementia consent to having sex? Leslie’s instincts now are narrowed to the primal: food, water, sleep, and, naturally, sex. So where do all these leftover feelings go when the body containing them is now only a vessel for a going mind?

Martin insists that Leslie — a once-celebrated and very talented painter now slowly going mute, mentally and emotionally and physically — is enjoying these encounters. They’ve been married for 19 years, after all, and when Amanda calls the police and introduces authorities into the situation, the couple is suddenly torn asunder. Then arise questions about whether they should continue to be separated and whether to place Leslie in a home.

Which is eventually what happens, and where Leslie forms an inappropriate bond with another patient to fill the Martin void. Writer/director Hammer, though, downplays the melodrama inherent to this scenario, even while shooting sequences, whether in Martin and Leslie’s apartment or in various hospitals, with a bracing handheld intimacy. (Cinematographer Adolpho Veloso, meanwhile, bathes London in a beautifully faded daylight.) Far from sterilely composed, a rape kit examination forced upon Leslie is harrowing and demeaning, especially as she has no idea what’s going on and no clue why a speculum is being inserted into her. In what world could Martin have raped his wife?

Binoche, who has been giving committed and emotionally controlled performances for years lately, including in films by Haneke, gives one of her most unsentimental and gripping performances at this stage in her career in “Queen at Sea.” An emotional phone call to her soon-to-be ex-husband lays bare to blanched vulnerability as she dials the last person she would prefer not to call, but the one she is forced to anyway. Interior lives outside those determined by this situation may be lacking, but Leslie’s isn’t. Amanda’s mother seems to activate when given the chance to paint at a nursing home, an aseptic and terrible place for which everyone in the family seems to be awkwardly auditioning.

The great British actor Courtenay, most recently memorable in the similarly memory-impaired marriage portrait “45 Years” opposite Charlotte Rampling, is quite devastating as a husband scrambling for answers and to legitimize his own place in Leslie’s life. The one element that doesn’t quite land, and seems quite literally chopped into the film, is Florence Hunt as Amanda’s daughter. Hammer seems to be trying to signal that she may be headed for her own future mental ruin by intercutting her first romance with scenes of Martin and Leslie’s last. It’s a noble idea, but it ends up feeling like scraps from an earlier draft.

Ultimately, though, anyone who’s endured what Amanda, or Leslie, or Martin do in this movie will find something to relate to and feel toward. Hammer spares no hard truths and offers no pat feelings with regard to how these people are bound to end up and what dementia ultimately does to them. Let’s just say hope is at a shortage. But the actors help carry Hammer’s message — and make it unforgettable.

Grade: B+

“Queen at Sea” premiered at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. Greenwich Entertainment opens the film starting Friday, October 30.

entry.title: ‘Clayface’ Tops the Box Office with $24 Million. What Does It Signal About DC Studios’ Latest Reboot?
entry.summary: 'Clayface' tops the box office with a decent $24 Million. What do its results signal for James Gunn and Peter Safran's DC revival?
entry.content:
“Clayface,” a body-horror film based on a little-known comic book, opened to $24 million, a middling result for DC Studios, which is in year two of its mixed-bag theatrical revival.

On the one hand, the gross isn’t bad considering that the title character is a niche player and the gory genre isn’t associated with the spandex set. On the other, it’s slightly below projections, which predicted that “Clayface” would open to between $25 million to $30 million. It was enough to hold off the second weekend of A24’s “You Can See Everything,” which earned $19.5 million. It also helps that “Clayface” is cheaper than most comic book movies, carrying a price tag of $44 million. It may not be a profit-generating machine, but it won’t lose money either.

Related Stories
Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores Huge $19.5 Million Second Weekend
Watch the ‘Buddy’ Team Explain How They Made the World Fall in Love with a Murderous Unicorn

That wasn’t the case with “Supergirl,” the previous film in the universe that James Gunn and Peter Safran have been building since they took the reins at DC. “Supergirl” was a disaster, losing an estimated $80 million to $120 million. It also received a critical drubbing. “Clayface” fared better in that respect too. It stands at 75% “fresh” on Rotten Tomatoes compared to “Supergirl’s” 52% “rotten” rating. So far, last summer’s “Superman,” which Gunn wrote and directed, is the most successful example of their quippy, poppy approach. It earned $618.7 million globally and was widely embraced by critics. The company’s streaming shows, which include “Lanterns” and “Peacemaker,” have been better received.

But nothing DC has produced under Gunn and Safran has come close to the box office heights enjoyed by Christopher Nolan’s “The Dark Knight” trilogy, the first “Aquaman,” or “Wonder Woman.” Two of Nolan’s “Dark Knight” movies topped $1 billion, as did “Aquaman,” while “Wonder Woman” earned $823.9 million. When Gunn and Safran were enlisted to revitalize DC, the brand was struggling with consistency, with films like “Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom” and “The Flash” collapsing in spectacular fashion — they were little seen and little enjoyed. The product the pair has produced has improved on that low bar, even as DC’s more recent efforts have yet to deliver the same gloriously demented pleasures of Gunn’s “Guardians of the Galaxy” films. Safran, a veteran producer whose credits include “The Conjuring” franchise, is seen as the business brains of the operation, while Gunn speaks comic book and is tasked with charting the creative vision.

Looking ahead, DC will bring back some of its headliners. “The Batman: Part II” will open in theaters in 2028, while Gunn will return to the world of Superman with next summer’s “Man of Tomorrow.” Both films seem poised to connect with audiences.

Ultimately, Gunn and Safran may just have the misfortune of leading a comic book empire at a time when audiences are getting much more selective about their costumed heroes. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” is the highest-grossing film of the year, having earned $2.5 billion, but that film features one of the most iconic comic book characters in history. Likewise, “Avengers: Doomsday” is expected to be a blockbuster when it opens in December, but it boasts Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans returning to the MCU. Outside of those Tiffany brands, even Marvel, which DC so clearly wants to emulate, has struggled. The company’s attempts to build up a new group of Avengers, such as “Thunderbolts,” “The Fantastic Four: First Steps,” “The Eternals,” and “The Marvels,” have been box office disappointments, if not outright bombs. If the king of comic book universes is struggling, maybe it’s wrong to hope for more from Gunn and Safran. In that kind of atmosphere, “Clayface” may count as a win, modest though its victory may be.

entry.title: Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores Huge $19.5 Million Second Weekend
entry.summary: A24's 'You Can See Everything' showed no signs of slowing down, earning a massive $19.5 million in its second weekend.
entry.content:
Audiences continued to flock to “You Can See Everything,” as the twisty documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes captured the zeitgeist and saw its grosses increase in its second weekend. The A24 film earned $19.5 million over its sophomore frame, a 25% improvement from its $15.6 million opening. Few movies see their grosses rise like that.

However, the film expanded its theater count, which helped lift ticket sales. “You Can See Everything” is playing in 2,655 theaters, up from the 855 it debuted on the previous weekend. Its popularity is remarkable considering that “You Can See Everything” is a three-hour documentary that is playing like a broadly commercial feature. It helped that A24 cloaked the film in secrecy, convincing audiences that the only way to avoid spoilers was to buy a ticket.

Related Stories
Watch the ‘Buddy’ Team Explain How They Made the World Fall in Love with a Murderous Unicorn
Quentin Tarantino Surprises Fans with an Early Look at ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’

Produced for a mere $7 million, “You Can See Everything” has grossed $45.1 million, positioning it to be one of the most successful non-fiction films in history. Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” an anti-Bush treatise released in the midst of the contentious 2004 presidential election, remains the highest-grossing documentary with just over $222 million in receipts. “You Can See Everything” has easily topped “Melania,” which had been the year’s highest-grossing doc with its $16.3 million gross. That look at the gilded life of America’s First Lady was a lot less profitable given that Jeff Bezos and Amazon MGM Studios shelled out $40 million for the rights (they love non-fiction filmmaking!).

Will the box office success propel “You Can See Everything” and its directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into the Oscar race? The jury is still out on that, though awards prognosticators have written many, many, many words on the subject.

Even if the documentary branch shuts Fielder and Oppenheim out or “You Can See Everything” fails to be the first documentary to land a Best Picture nomination, it will go down as a massive hit for A24, extending a sizzling streak at the box office. This year, the studio released “Backrooms,” the biggest blockbuster in its history with a $400 million global haul, as well as winners like “Primetime” and “The Drama.” And it did by proving that audiences will turn up in theaters for more than just superhero flicks and sequels. Turns out, they’re interested in Silicon Valley flameouts too.

entry.title: Watch the ‘Buddy’ Team Explain How They Made the World Fall in Love with a Murderous Unicorn
entry.summary: At IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit, Tracy Rosenblum, Jamie King, and unpacked the formula behind one of 2026's breakout hits, 'Buddy.'
entry.content:
Sometimes, a movie appears seemingly out of nowhere and instantly captures the zeitgeist. In 2026, one of those movies was “Buddy.”

Casper Kelly’s horror comedy about a ’90s TV show mascot with a dark side captures the nostalgia subversion that made his Adult Swim projects like “Too Many Cooks” into viral hits. But what separates “Buddy” from so many other movies about cuddly villains is the emotional depth lurking below the surface. The many facets of Buddy the Unicorn — his humor, his charisma, his sadism, and his remorse for his actions — allowed Roadside Attractions to mount a unique marketing campaign that introduced audiences to the character before letting them know he had a homicidal streak. The campaign created a false memory that led many of us to wonder if “Buddy” was actually a cancelled TV show we had forgotten about. It ensured that we were invested in the character before we even knew what the film was about.

Related Stories
Quentin Tarantino Surprises Fans with an Early Look at ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’
‘Color Book’ Director David Fortune Used Ice Cold Showers to Practice His AT&T Untold Stories Award Pitch — Watch

At IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles, “Buddy” producer Tracy Rosenblum, co-writer Jamie King, and Roadside Attractions head of digital marketing Melissa Yerou joined us for a conversation about the years of behind-the-scenes work that goes into an overnight success.

The project was originally conceived as a way to put Kelly’s distinct brand of comedy into a feature film. King was brought in as a co-writer to help Kelly fit his wild sensibilities into a movie format, and used his recent experience writing Disney movies to ground the story with enough heart to reach a wider audience.

“I knew, as a fan of Casper’s and all of his Adult Swim work, that he would make it really funny. And I knew my friends at BoulderLight would make it really scary. So I thought that if I can help bring that heart element, that checks all three boxes, and that’s what makes a great movie,” King said, adding that he and Kelly worked hard to ensure Buddy came across as a three dimensional character who contained both light and darkness. ““He was always very clear that Buddy was not one of those mascot horror movies you’ve seen before, where Buddy is just a fuzzy version of a slasher villain… He’s someone who could be a good person, but he’s just gone down the wrong road.”

“I resent you calling him a homicidal maniac,” Rosenblum said with a laugh. “He has depth, and he has shame, and he’s not a good guy, but I think that’s what makes him special.”

The character was so thoroughly developed that Yerou and her team could hit the ground running on a marketing campaign. They quickly found success by having Buddy interact with classic ’90s brands on social media, as audiences fell in love with the voice that King and Kelly worked so hard to refine.

“We followed Care Bears and Barney and all these tried and true properties. We just thought ‘What if we had Buddy bust into the conversations, how would they react?’” Yerou said. “At first we were responding to every single comment. We really wanted to heighten the engagement, and at a certain point people were commenting just because they wanted Buddy to respond.”

Watch the complete panel in the video above.

entry.title: Quentin Tarantino Surprises Fans With an Early Look at ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’
entry.summary: Following a screening of 'Once Upon a Time...in Hollywood,' the writer-director presented 17 minutes from 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth'
entry.content:
Last night the 40th annual AFI Fest held a special screening of “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood” at the Chinese Theatre with Quentin Tarantino in attendance. For the 900 or so Tarantino fans who packed the house, just seeing the director’s 2019 crowd-pleaser on the huge Chinese screen followed by a lively Tarantino Q&A would have been enough — but then Quentin had a surprise for the audience.

At the end of the post-screening discussion with moderator Jacqueline Coley, Coley asked Tarantino about “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” the highly anticipated holiday release that picks up on “Once Upon a Time” stuntman Cliff’s (Brad Pitt) life in Hollywood in the 1970s. Tarantino wrote the script but isn’t directing this time out, having handed the script off to frequent Pitt collaborator David Fincher. Tarantino responded to Coley’s question about the new film with an answer that immediately sent the audience at the Chinese into a state of cinephilic ecstasy.

Related Stories
‘Color Book’ Director David Fortune Used Ice Cold Showers to Practice His AT&T Untold Stories Award Pitch — Watch
‘They’re Still Humans Like the Rest of Us’: Watch the ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Directors Discuss Relating to Extreme Athletes

“I could talk a little bit about ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,'” Tarantino said. “Or…I could show you the first 17 minutes.” With that, the crowd went insane, the lights went out, and the attendees at AFI Fest got to be the first audience to get a substantive look at Tarantino and Fincher’s new opus.

Based on the footage screened, “Cliff Booth” finds Tarantino returning to his roots; like “True Romance,” “Reservoir Dogs,” and “Pulp Fiction,” it’s a crime movie heavily influenced by novelists like Elmore Leonard (who Tarantino adapted for one of his best films, “Jackie Brown”) and Raymond Chandler. It also presents a darker Cliff Booth than the one we saw in “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood,” a version closer to the more cold-blooded, almost sociopathic Booth introduced in Tarantino’s novelization of “Once Upon a Time” than the amiable (albeit wife-murdering) fellow from the movie.

When we left Cliff Booth at the end of “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood,” he was coming off of a sojourn in Italy to double his pal Rick Dalton (Leonardo DiCaprio); as the new film begins in June 1977, his primary connection to the film industry is a job as a projectionist at the New Beverly Cinema. (A fun in-joke that got a big laugh from the AFI Fest audience, most of whom were probably well aware that Tarantino now owns that theater.) Booth’s real profession seems to be as a kind of shady bag man and fixer, though the 17 minutes we saw at the Chinese wasn’t enough to give a strong sense of where the plot will go.

What it did give was some choice Tarantino dialogue, particularly in “Soul Brothers Die Hard,” a Blaxploitation film-within-the-film starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II (and presumably unrelated to the 1973 movie “Brother on the Run,” which was released in some markets under the alternate title of “Soul Brothers Die Hard,” though with Tarantino you never know what kind of subterranean connection might exist). There’s also a promising relationship between Cliff and his father, a pawn shop proprietor played by Peter Weller, and enough period-accurate production design and pop culture references to assure the audience that “Cliff Booth” will be as rich in nostalgic pleasures of the late 1970s as “Once Upon a Time” was for the late 1960s.

The Q&A with Tarantino that preceded the “Cliff Booth” footage didn’t have much new information (especially for anyone who has read Jay Glennie’s doorstop of a coffee table book, “The Making of ‘Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood'”) but was fun nevertheless, thanks to Tarantino’s typical loquacity and Coley’s thoughtful line of questioning. Tarantino revealed the most personally meaningful piece of casting in a film filled with great performances — including supporting turns by multiple actors (Austin Butler, Mikey Madison, Sydney Sweeney) who have blown up in the seven years since.

“The casting that to me was the most meaningful ended up not being in the movie,” Tarantino said, recalling that Burt Reynolds was originally cast in the role of George Spahn. “He said yes, and we became friendly, but he passed away before we could make the film. But we did get to rehearse with him and do the script reading with him, so actually, the last performance Burt Reynolds ever gave was as George Spahn in the script reading.” (Bruce Dern would ultimately play the role in the finished film.)

Tarantino also referenced some of the many Easter eggs in the film, like the fact that the voice of the Pan Am flight attendant who waits on Rick Dalton on his flight back to Italy was Margot Robbie — a nod to her early work on the short-lived television series Pan Am. Tarantino also provided an extensive history of the “Canadian tuxedo” worn by Brad Pitt, a look often recognized as a tribute to Tom Laughlin in “Billy Jack.” According to Tarantino, however, the reference goes way deeper.

 ”It doesn’t just look like Billy Jack’s outfit; it is Billy Jack’s outfit,” Tarantino said, explaining that in the mythology he created for “Once Upon a Time…in Hollywood,” Cliff was working as a double for actor Jeff Cooper on “Born Losers,” the first film in which Tom Laughlin appeared as Billy Jack. In Tarantino’s backstory, Laughlin’s stunt double twisted his ankle, and Cliff took his place for the last week of the shoot — and for his work, he was given Billy Jack’s outfit that he wore in the movie, plus 25 bucks.

It was clear from Tarantino’s deep dive into the thinking behind elements like this costume and the set decoration in Cliff’s trailer (much of which, like many other items in the film, came from the director’s own personal collection), that behind every detail there’s a wealth of creation that never makes its way to the screen.

“The thing is, I’ve got nothing to do but invest in this mythology,” Tarantino said. “I invested in it before I did the movie, and I’ve invested in it in the years since I’ve done the movie. The audience doesn’t need to know everything. But it’s nice if I know everything.”

AFI Fest runs through Sunday night in Hollywood. “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” opens theatrically from Netflix on November 25.

entry.title: ‘Color Book’ Director David Fortune Used Ice Cold Showers to Practice His AT&T Untold Stories Award Pitch — Watch
entry.summary: Watch our conversation with AT&T Untold Stories Award winner David Fortune at IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit.
entry.content:
The AT&T Untold Stories Award is the world’s largest filmmaking award of its kind. Each year, hundreds of filmmakers apply to be considered for a prize that includes $1.2 million and a network of mentorship and support to help them make a film. Those candidates are narrowed down to five finalists who get a chance to pitch their film in front of a packed audience and a panel of judges at the Tribeca Festival. Win them over, and you might get a chance to bring your cinematic vision to life.

David Fortune knows just how impactful the prize can be. The filmmaker, who won the 2023 AT&T Untold Stories Award, used the grant to make his 2024 feature “Color Book,” which is now streaming on Netflix.

Related Stories
‘They’re Still Humans Like the Rest of Us’: Watch the ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Directors Discuss Relating to Extreme Athletes
Yes, That’s a Wicker Penis: Inside Alexander Skarsgård’s Wild ‘Wicker’ Transformation

The film, which tells the story of a single father raising a son with Down syndrome who takes him to his first baseball game, is exactly the kind of project that the program exists to support. It tells a nuanced story about Black single parenthood that we had seldom seen on screen, all filtered through the voice of one distinctly talented filmmaker.

During a conversation at IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit, presented by AT&T, Fortune explained how he approached an opportunity that turned out to be life-changing.

“I would say preparation,” Fortune said when asked to give advice to future contestants. “You can’t control if you win or lose, but you can control how you prepare. I knew I was gonna be nervous as hell, but even in my nervousness I wanted to make sure I was able to pitch correctly and present myself in a way that gave me my best chance to win. I just wanted to be the most prepared person in the room.”

That preparation saw him pushing his body to his limits to ensure that nothing would shake him when it was time to pitch in front of a crowd.

“I jumped in the shower, and I put it on the most ice cold level you could put it in. And I jumped in and said ‘Say your pitch now,’ he said with a laugh. “I had to pitch with hypothermia! Because if you can’t pitch in a chokehold, how are you going to pitch on stage?”

Of course, Fortune’s process is not the only approach that can work. The presentation also featured a video message from Lilian T. Mehrel, who won the 2024 competition and used the prize money to make her feature debut “Honeyjooon.” She recalled her own process of pitching her film, and the validation that she received when she was finally able to show the finished product to audiences.

“That day that I pitched, I knew if I could make audiences laugh and cry and feel emotional and get a sense of the auteur cinematic comedy stamp that is my voice, then I would win. And I did!” Mehrel said, adding that the film went on to play over 50 festivals. “Being in the audience, hearing people laugh and get emotional together… it was just this electric experience. It gave me the fuel to know that this film needs to be released in theaters.”

Watch the complete conversation with Fortune in the video above.

entry.title: ‘They’re Still Humans Like the Rest of Us’: Watch the ‘Everest: The Other Side’ Directors Discuss Relating to Extreme Athletes
entry.summary: At IndieWire's Art of the Doc event, Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin explained what draws them to risk-taking subjects.
entry.content:
Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin know a thing or two about extreme athletes. From the daring rock climbing of “Free Solo” to their new film “Everest: The Other Side,” which follows Jim Morrison’s attempts to fulfill his late wife Hilaree Nelson’s dream of skiing down the world’s tallest mountain, the documentarians love to capture fearless people drawn to extreme challenges.

During a conversation about “Everest” with IndieWire features writer Alison Foreman at our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, the filmmakers discussed what draws them to the subject matter over and over again.

“In all our films, you think you’re seeing these exceptional, extraordinary, extreme athletes. But at the end of the day they’re still human beings like the rest of us,” Chin said. “What I’m interested in bridging that gap where people feel like they can’t relate to people out there doing these things. But the story is really human, and this film is about very human experiences. Even though they’re climbing and skiiing the most extreme places in the world.”

Related Stories
Yes, That’s a Wicker Penis: Inside Alexander Skarsgård’s Wild ‘Wicker’ Transformation
‘Marie Antoinette’ at 20: Sofia Coppola on How the Film Almost Broke Her, the Critical Backlash, and Paying Tribute to Mom

Vasarhelyi also emphasized the fact that each documentary subject is a different person with their own unique story to tell. In the case of Nelson, she saw someone who was deeply goal-oriented but lacked the grand romanticizations about her sport that drive so many other athletes. She saw the adventurer as a fellow parent who lived a fairly normal life when she wasn’t pushing herself to scale the world’s highest peaks.

“I had met a lot of extreme athletes, but Hilaree had a candor to her vocation that I hadn’t heard before,” Vasarhelyi said. “It’s not romantic. She says in the film, ‘I know it’s just a mountain, but it’s everything to me. And I’m like a dog with a bone.’ And I understand that.”

entry.title: Yes, That’s a Wicker Penis: Inside Alexander Skarsgård’s Wild ‘Wicker’ Transformation
entry.summary: The costume designers, art director, and prosthetic makeup designer of “Wicker” took IndieWire through the process of creating the "Wicker" Husband.
entry.content:
You’ll never look at a wicker basket the same way after “Wicker”. Based on Ursula Wills-Jones’s short story “The Wicker Husband”, the raunchy period comedy follows an outcast Fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) commissioning a master Basket Weaver (Peter Dinklage) to make her a wicker husband. The result is a man entirely woven of wicker whose dedication to his wife and romance is absolute; of course, it’s a role for Alexander Skarsgård.

Transforming the 6’4″ Swede into the Wicker Husband required not actual magic, but something very close to it. Art director and prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley, as well as makeup and hair designer Sarah Rubano from Wētā Workshop, and their teams collaborated with directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer on creating a fully practical suit and full facial prosthetic makeup so that Skarsgård could move and emote as freely as the romance novel-inspired poster for “Wicker” promises.

Related Stories
‘Marie Antoinette’ at 20: Sofia Coppola on How the Film Almost Broke Her, the Critical Backlash, and Paying Tribute to Mom
Watch Bill Hader Explain the Many Influences That Led to His First Film, ‘They Know’

“The success of the film hinged on the quality of the makeup itself; if you were going to be invested in this film, that character needed to be believable in that world,” Dunckley told IndieWire.

Over 18 months, the Wētā team researched, developed, and manufactured “Wicker”’s co-protagonist, developing an entirely new way to make prosthetic makeup in the process. “Traditional materials wouldn’t be viable because wicker’s geometry is just far too complex; it’s really unmoldable,” Dunckley said. “We had a very good understanding of the cutting edge of 3D printing technology, but we still didn’t know how exactly to do this; none of the hardware is intended to be used this way.”

Weaving the Wicker Husband

The timing was serendipitous; Wētā textiles and weaving team had just come off “Avatar”, where they had been weaving costumes for the Na’vi for years. Some jumped over to “Wicker” to help refine the creative process for the Wicker Husband. Explaining the creation process, Dunckley said: “Our concept team blocked out shapes, [head weaver Jasmin Van Lith] would do a physical weave sample; we’d incorporate that back into the 2D artwork. Then we’d do a 3D model of that weave, print out a test piece, and do a make-up test and see if it behaved in the way we wanted, then go back to the sampling.”

Dunckley shared that they aimed for this wicker weaving to replicate muscle fiber; it had to be tight enough to hold together but loose enough for the strands to move and flex. With the wicker weaving samples perfected, Rubano shared: “There were 50 individual 3D-printed body pieces from the neck down anchored onto very thin spandex or power mesh for the fabricated suit. Then the suit’s hood goes over his head and over [Skarsgård’s] chin so that as he moves his head, the neck moves along with him.”

For the face, they also applied individually crafted pieces: wicker ears, wicker lips, a jaw piece, a larger forehead, cheekbones, and a nose, which Rubano likens to “a Batman mask piece.” Then there’s the wig, eyelashes, and facial hair. Rubano explains these components are “made out of muka, a New Zealand flax plant, strands that are teased and shredded, and then knotted onto the weave, just like human hair onto lace.”

Wētā is famous for its monsters and sci-fi creatures, so making a romantic lead gave the creatives a unique challenge. “We weren’t making a human being or a creature of flesh and blood,” Dunckley highlighted. Rubano added the other layer of difficulty: “Alexander’s going to be completely covered up, but we need his essence to shine through.” Maintaining Skarsgård’s likeness meant ensuring the utmost practicality of the costume: it would hide Skarsgård’s skin but not his expressions.

The costume was almost entirely practical; only a few details required CGI. One of which was sunlight peeking through the woven gaps of the Wicker Husband. “From the elbows down, [Skarsgård wore] fitted blue spandex under his forearms, so VFX was possible for very key moments,” Robano said. “The only other effects were the removal of a bit of pinkness in the tear ducts, waterline and around his eyeball.”

Dressing the Wicker Husband

Though Wētā created the face and torso of the Wicker Husband, a different pair of hands was required for below the waist. Hungarian costume designer duo Tóth András Dániel and Attila Godena-Juhász (who previously worked on “The Uprising” and “Martin Scorsese Presents: The Saints”) worked closely with Dunckley and Rubano to ensure continuity with costumes, silhouettes, and the wicker prosthetics.

“One week before the shoot started, the directors said we should see [the Wicker Husband] naked,” Dániel said. That triggered a fast-tracked costume project to create pants that seamlessly mimic the prosthetics. “We invented a technique: printing on an elastic base with a special paint that, if you treat it with heat, it’s three-dimensional… wicker penis included, Alex made a joke that because he came to the workshop for several fittings, and he really wanted to know the size of his [penis]. It was a lot of fun,” Dániel said.

Their small team then hand-painted and shaded every wicker detail for realism. “Unfortunately, it’s not so visible when he’s walking into the lake, but it was very cool,” Godena-Juhász said.

Beyond the wicker pants, Dániel and Godena-Juhász also dressed the Wicker Husband. They were granted freedom with costumes, not restricted by place or time. “If you need to create a village, a universe that [doesn’t really exist], you need to use references that aren’t known to the world; that’s why we ended up using Hungarian folk art and garments as an inspiration, because outside of Hungary, no one really knows what it looks like,” Dániel said.

Alongside this, the pair note that they also moodboarded inspiration from 17th-, 18th-, and 19th-century styles, textures, and colours before designing every costume component of this otherworldly erotic fantasy.

Then came time to get Skarsgård kitted up. “Alex is a big guy, and [when] Wētā added the prosthetics, they made him even bigger; it was such a nice silhouette,” Dániel said. “We made every piece of garment he’s wearing a little bit smaller, like it’s the suit you wore in high school and grew out of; the sleeves and hemline of the pants are short, and the waistline is not at the waist.”

Godena-Juhász added: “Also, everybody wanted to save time, and not apply the whole [wicker] body, so we made a padded under-layer. So even if he’s wearing the shirt, without the prosthetics, the silhouette remains the same.”

The Wicker Husband’s full-scale grand reveal comes after he knocks on doors around the village to borrow clothes, resulting in a snug-fitting wedding suit paired with brown laced shoes from a Hungarian shoemaker. “We ended up using this dark blue-greyish, very fancy tweed,” Dániel noted. “The cut of the three-piece suit is referring to the 17th-century menswear.” That refined seriousness, paired with the skin-tight fit, creates an image of both sophistication and sexiness.

The latter is elevated in a later scene where the villager crowd parts, in shock and awe, to watch the Fisherwoman and Wicker Husband’s sensual dancing. “We decided to lose the jacket for that scene because it’s far more elevated and easier for him to dance without the jacket,” Dániel recalled. “The cut of the shirt was quite oversized, matching perfectly with Olivia’s blouse. It’s so romantic.”

The Wicker Husband’s presence — his brooding desire, and the spectacle driving the whole town wild with horny jealousy — is a majestic demonstration of cinematic craft from Dániel and Godena-Juhász and Dunckley and Rubano.

Thankfully, no one got splinters.
